nodes.statement: Computers represent a radical novelty.
nodes.span: the assumption that computers represent a radical novelty
nodes.status_reason: stated as an assumption the author makes

nodes.statement: The usual method of coping with novelty via metaphors and analogies breaks down when faced with a sharp discontinuity.
nodes.span: in the case of a sharp discontinuity, however, the method breaks down
nodes.status_reason: follows from the reader's understanding of metaphors

nodes.statement: Coping with radical novelty requires approaching it with a blank mind and consciously refusing to link it to the familiar.
nodes.span: approach the radical novelty with a blank mind, consciously refusing to try to link it
nodes.status_reason: follows from the failure of analogies

nodes.statement: Radical novelties are so disturbing that people tend to suppress, ignore, or deny them.
nodes.span: radical novelties are so disturbing that they tend to be suppressed or ignored
nodes.status_reason: follows from the difficulty of the required blank mind

nodes.statement: Gauss suppressed his discovery of non-Euclidean geometry out of fear.
nodes.span: decided to suppress his discovery of non-Euclidean geometry
nodes.status_reason: historical anecdote provided as evidence

nodes.statement: The mathematical community assumes that doing mathematics will remain the same type of mental activity it has always been.
nodes.span: the mathematical community has never challenged its tacit assumption that doing mathematics will remain very much the same
nodes.status_reason: observation of the mathematical community provided as evidence

nodes.statement: Educational practices constantly try to disguise exciting novelties as familiar things.
nodes.span: constantly try to present everything that could be an exciting novelty as something as familiar as possible
nodes.status_reason: observation of educational practices provided as evidence

nodes.statement: Automatic computers embody not just one, but two radical novelties.
nodes.span: automatic computers embody not only one radical novelty but two of them
nodes.status_reason: follows from the assumption that computers are a radical novelty

nodes.statement: The first radical novelty is the gigantic ratio of scale that requires programmers to use unprecedentedly deep conceptual hierarchies.
nodes.span: think in terms of conceptual hierarchies that are much deeper than a single mind ever needed to face before
nodes.status_reason: follows from the physical reality of computing scale

nodes.statement: The second radical novelty is that computers are large-scale digital devices where the smallest perturbations can have drastic consequences.
nodes.span: the automatic computer is our first large-scale digital device
nodes.status_reason: follows from the discrete nature of computers

nodes.statement: The evidence that computing's novelties are radical lies in the doomed efforts to hide or deny the unfamiliar.
nodes.span: strange phenomena as frantic —but, as we now know, doomed— efforts at hiding or denying the frighteningly unfamiliar
nodes.status_reason: follows from the tendency to deny radical novelties

nodes.statement: Software engineering is a doomed discipline that tries to teach people how to program if they cannot.
nodes.span: software engineering has accepted as its charter "How to program if you cannot."
nodes.status_reason: observation of software engineering provided as evidence

nodes.statement: Measuring programmer productivity in lines of code is a reassuring illusion that programs are like other devices.
nodes.span: measuring "programmer productivity" in terms of "number of lines of code produced per month"
nodes.status_reason: observation of productivity metrics provided as evidence

nodes.statement: Software engineers continue to refine testing strategies even though testing can never demonstrate the absence of bugs.
nodes.span: program testing may convincingly demonstrate the presence of bugs, but can never demonstrate their absence
nodes.status_reason: observation of testing practices provided as evidence

nodes.statement: Artificial Intelligence is popular because it makes the computer less frightening by simulating a familiar noncomputer.
nodes.span: the frightening computer becomes less frightening if it is used only to simulate a familiar noncomputer
nodes.status_reason: observation of AI's popularity provided as evidence

nodes.statement: A program is an abstract symbol manipulator that becomes concrete when a computer is supplied to it.
nodes.span: the program is an abstract symbol manipulator, which can be turned into a concrete one by supplying a computer
nodes.status_reason: follows from the discrete nature of computers

nodes.statement: Programs are elaborate formulae from a formal system, and the programmer's task is to derive that formula.
nodes.span: programs or —to use somewhat more general terminology— usually rather elaborate formulae from some formal system
nodes.status_reason: follows from the definition of abstract symbol manipulators

nodes.statement: Computing science is concerned with the interplay between mechanized and human symbol manipulation.
nodes.span: computing science is —and will always be— concerned with the interplay between mechanized and human symbol manipulation
nodes.status_reason: follows from the programmer's task of deriving formulae

nodes.statement: We should clean up our language by calling a bug an error to put the blame on the programmer.
nodes.span: cleaning up our language by no longer calling a bug a bug but by calling it an error
nodes.status_reason: follows from the programmer's responsibility for the code

nodes.statement: We must never refer to parts of programs or equipment in anthropomorphic terminology.
nodes.span: never refer to parts of programs or pieces of equipment in an anthropomorphic terminology
nodes.status_reason: follows from the wastefulness of operational reasoning

nodes.statement: The anthropomorphic metaphor forces people to think about programs in terms of computational behaviors, which is a tremendous waste of mental effort.
nodes.span: operational reasoning is a tremendous waste of mental effort
nodes.status_reason: follows from the inefficiency of element-wise reasoning

nodes.statement: To demonstrate something about all elements of a large set, it is hopelessly inefficient to deal with elements individually; one must use the set's definition.
nodes.span: if we have to demonstrate something about all the elements of a large set, it is hopelessly inefficient
nodes.status_reason: follows from basic logic and set theory

nodes.statement: Proving that a mutilated chessboard cannot be covered by dominos is vastly simpler using a coloring argument than by exhaustively generating all placements.
nodes.span: each placement covers as many white squares as it covers black squares
nodes.status_reason: mathematical proof example provided as evidence

nodes.statement: Because a program defines a set of computations, we must deal with all possible computations by ignoring them and working with the program text.
nodes.span: deal with all computations possible under control of a given program by ignoring them and working with the program
nodes.status_reason: follows from the inefficiency of reasoning about individual computations

nodes.statement: A programming language is a formal system for which program execution provides only a model.
nodes.span: A programming language, with its formal syntax and with the proof rules that define its semantics, is a formal system
nodes.status_reason: follows from the need to work with program texts

nodes.statement: A program is half a conjecture, and the programmer must present complete conjectures as proven theorems.
nodes.span: The programmer's task is to present such complete conjectures as proven theorems.
nodes.status_reason: follows from viewing programming languages as formal systems

nodes.statement: An introductory programming course should teach boolean algebra, a clean imperative language defined by proof rules, and require students to formally prove their programs meet specifications without testing them.
nodes.span: his main task is to give a formal proof that the program he proposes meets the equally formal functional specification
nodes.status_reason: follows from the programmer's task to present proven theorems

nodes.statement: Such an introductory programming course has been successfully given to hundreds of college freshmen each year since the early 80s.
nodes.span: such an introductory programming course has successfully been given to hundreds of college freshmen each year
nodes.status_reason: historical fact about the course provided as evidence

nodes.statement: Students quickly discover that mastering the manipulation of uninterpreted formulae gives them immense power, rather than being frustrated.
nodes.span: he makes the exciting discovery that he is beginning to master the use of a tool that
nodes.status_reason: observation of student reactions provided as evidence
